questions.question: How many players from one team are on the court during a standard basketball game?
questions.explanation: Each basketball team has five players on the court at a time.

questions.question: How many players does a soccer team have on the field at one time, including the goalkeeper?
questions.explanation: A soccer team fields 11 players: 10 outfield players plus one goalkeeper.

questions.question: In tennis, what word is used to describe a score of zero?
questions.explanation: Tennis calls a score of zero "love" — for example, "15–love."

questions.question: How many holes are played in a standard full round of golf?
questions.explanation: A standard round of golf consists of 18 holes.

questions.question: How many interlocking rings appear on the Olympic flag?
questions.explanation: The five Olympic rings represent the union of the world's continents through sport.

questions.question: Which sport is played with a racket and a feathered or plastic shuttlecock?
questions.explanation: Badminton players hit a shuttlecock (also called a "birdie") over a net.

questions.question: In American football, how many points is a touchdown worth before any extra-point attempt?
questions.explanation: A touchdown is worth 6 points; the team can then try for 1 or 2 extra points.

questions.question: In baseball, how many strikes does it take for a batter to strike out?
questions.explanation: Three strikes and you're out! Four balls, on the other hand, earns a walk.

questions.question: Which country hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
questions.explanation: The first modern Olympics were held in Athens, Greece, honoring the ancient Games.

questions.question: About how long is an official marathon race?
questions.explanation: A marathon is 42.195 kilometers, or about 26.2 miles.

questions.question: In ten-pin bowling, what is it called when you knock down all ten pins with your first ball of a frame?
questions.explanation: Knocking down all ten pins on the first roll is a strike; doing it in two rolls is a spare.

questions.question: The traditional wrestling sport of sumo originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Sumo has been practiced in Japan for centuries and is closely tied to Shinto traditions.

questions.question: How many periods are played in a regulation NHL ice hockey game?
questions.explanation: An NHL game has three 20-minute periods.

questions.question: How many players are on each side in a standard game of cricket?
questions.explanation: A cricket team fields 11 players, just like soccer.

questions.question: In indoor volleyball, what is the maximum number of touches a team may use to return the ball (not counting a block)?
questions.explanation: Teams get up to three touches — often a bump, set, and spike — to send the ball back over the net.

questions.question: What is the highest possible score in a single game of ten-pin bowling?
questions.explanation: A perfect game is 12 strikes in a row, for a score of 300.

questions.question: The Tour de France is a famous race in which sport?
questions.explanation: The Tour de France is a multi-week professional cycling race held mostly in France.

questions.question: In an Olympic individual medley swimming race, which stroke is swum first?
questions.explanation: The individual medley order is butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, then freestyle.

questions.question: How often is the men's FIFA World Cup normally held?
questions.explanation: The FIFA World Cup is held every four years.

questions.question: Teams in which sport compete to win the Stanley Cup?
questions.explanation: The Stanley Cup is awarded to the NHL's championship team.

questions.question: How many U.S. senators does each state have?
questions.explanation: Every state has two senators, no matter its population.

questions.question: How many voting members are in the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: The House has 435 voting members, divided among the states by population.

questions.question: How long is a single term for a U.S. senator?
questions.explanation: Senators serve six-year terms, with about one-third of seats up for election every two years.

questions.question: How long is a single term for a member of the U.S. House of Representatives?
questions.explanation: Representatives serve two-year terms, so every House seat is up for election every two years.

questions.question: Who is the Commander in Chief of the U.S. armed forces?
questions.explanation: The Constitution makes the President the Commander in Chief of the military.

questions.question: Which branch of the U.S. government interprets the laws?
questions.explanation: The judicial branch — the courts — interprets laws and decides whether they follow the Constitution.

questions.question: How many justices sit on the U.S. Supreme Court?
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court has had nine justices — one Chief Justice and eight associates — since 1869.

questions.question: What is it called when the President rejects a bill passed by Congress?
questions.explanation: A veto lets the President reject a bill; Congress can try to override it.

questions.question: What fraction of votes in both the House and Senate is needed to override a presidential veto?
questions.explanation: Overriding a veto takes a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress.

questions.question: If the President can no longer serve, who is first in line to become President?
questions.explanation: The Vice President is first in the presidential line of succession.

questions.question: How many electoral votes does a candidate need to win the U.S. presidency?
questions.explanation: There are 538 electoral votes in total, so a majority is 270.

questions.question: What is the name for a system where power is shared between a national government and state governments?
questions.explanation: Federalism divides power between the national government and the states.

questions.question: Who serves as the President of the U.S. Senate?
questions.explanation: The Vice President presides over the Senate and can cast a vote to break a tie.

questions.question: In a parliamentary system such as the United Kingdom's, what is the head of government usually called?
questions.explanation: In parliamentary systems the Prime Minister leads the government, usually as head of the largest party.

questions.question: What is the minimum age to vote in U.S. federal elections?
questions.explanation: U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections starting at age 18.

questions.question: How many amendments are in the U.S. Constitution?
questions.explanation: The U.S. Constitution currently has 27 ratified amendments.

questions.question: What are the first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution called?
questions.explanation: The Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, protects key individual freedoms.

questions.question: What is the introduction to the U.S. Constitution called?
questions.explanation: The Preamble explains the purposes of the Constitution, such as forming "a more perfect Union."

questions.question: What are the first three words of the U.S. Constitution?
questions.explanation: "We the People" signals that the government's power comes from its citizens.

questions.question: Which amendment protects freedom of speech, religion, and the press?
questions.explanation: The First Amendment protects speech, religion, press, assembly, and petition.

questions.question: In what year was the U.S. Constitution signed?
questions.explanation: Delegates signed the Constitution on September 17, 1787.

questions.question: In which city was the U.S. Constitution written and signed?
questions.explanation: The Constitutional Convention met at Independence Hall in Philadelphia.

questions.question: Which amendment abolished slavery in the United States?
questions.explanation: The 13th Amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery.

questions.question: Which amendment guaranteed women the right to vote?
questions.explanation: The 19th Amendment, ratified in 1920, prohibits denying the vote based on sex.

questions.question: Which amendment lowered the voting age to 18?
questions.explanation: The 26th Amendment, ratified in 1971, set the voting age at 18.

questions.question: Which article of the Constitution creates the legislative branch (Congress)?
questions.explanation: Article I sets up Congress; Article II covers the President, and Article III the courts.

questions.question: According to the Constitution, what is the minimum age to become President?
questions.explanation: A President must be at least 35 years old and a natural-born citizen.

questions.question: Which amendment limits a President to being elected twice?
questions.explanation: The 22nd Amendment, ratified in 1951, limits Presidents to two elected terms.

questions.question: Which amendment protects people against unreasonable searches and seizures?
questions.explanation: The Fourth Amendment generally requires a warrant based on probable cause.

questions.question: What fraction of the states must ratify a proposed amendment for it to become part of the Constitution?
questions.explanation: Three-fourths of the states (38 of 50) must ratify an amendment.

questions.question: Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, and others, is often called the Festival of what?
questions.explanation: Diwali is the Festival of Lights, celebrated with oil lamps, candles, and fireworks.

questions.question: Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead), a celebration honoring loved ones who have passed, is most closely associated with which country?
questions.explanation: Día de los Muertos is a Mexican tradition featuring altars called ofrendas, marigolds, and sugar skulls.

questions.question: What is the name of the traditional Japanese art of folding paper into shapes?
questions.explanation: Origami comes from the Japanese words "ori" (folding) and "kami" (paper).

questions.question: How many animal signs are in the Chinese zodiac?
questions.explanation: The Chinese zodiac has 12 animals that rotate in a 12-year cycle.

questions.question: Flamenco, a passionate style of music and dance, comes from which country?
questions.explanation: Flamenco developed in Andalusia, in southern Spain.

questions.question: Kimchi, a spicy fermented vegetable dish, is a staple of which country's cuisine?
questions.explanation: Kimchi, often made from napa cabbage, is central to Korean cooking.

questions.question: The Māori are the Indigenous Polynesian people of which country?
questions.explanation: The Māori are the Indigenous people of Aotearoa New Zealand.

questions.question: Holi, a joyful spring festival from India, is famous for people throwing what at each other?
questions.explanation: Holi, the Festival of Colors, celebrates spring with bright colored powders called gulal.

questions.question: The famous Oktoberfest celebration began in which German city?
questions.explanation: Oktoberfest started in Munich in 1810 to celebrate a royal wedding.

questions.question: Machu Picchu, a mountaintop city in Peru, was built by which civilization?
questions.explanation: The Inca built Machu Picchu in the Andes Mountains in the 1400s.

questions.question: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
questions.explanation: Mandarin Chinese has more native speakers than any other language.

questions.question: Kente, a colorful handwoven cloth, originated in which country?
questions.explanation: Kente cloth comes from the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana.

questions.question: The Taj Mahal, one of the world's most famous buildings, is located in which country?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal stands in Agra, India, and was completed in the mid-1600s.

questions.question: What is the name of the traditional Japanese robe-like garment tied with a sash called an obi?
questions.explanation: The kimono is a traditional Japanese garment worn with an obi sash.

questions.question: The world-famous Carnival in Rio de Janeiro takes place in which country?
questions.explanation: Rio's Carnival features samba schools, parades, and huge street parties.

questions.question: The didgeridoo is a traditional wind instrument of the Aboriginal peoples of which country?
questions.explanation: The didgeridoo was developed by Aboriginal peoples of northern Australia.

questions.question: During the month of Ramadan, many Muslims fast during which part of the day?
questions.explanation: Fasting during Ramadan lasts from dawn to sunset, and the fast is broken with a meal called iftar.

questions.question: For how many nights is the Jewish holiday of Hanukkah celebrated?
questions.explanation: Hanukkah lasts eight nights, with one more candle lit on the menorah each night.

questions.question: Phở, a noodle soup made with broth and herbs, is a famous dish from which country?
questions.explanation: Phở is a Vietnamese soup of rice noodles, broth, herbs, and often beef or chicken.

questions.question: Matryoshka dolls — wooden dolls that nest inside one another — are a traditional craft of which country?
questions.explanation: Matryoshka nesting dolls were first made in Russia in the 1890s.

questions.question: What is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Pacific is the largest and deepest ocean, covering about one-third of Earth's surface.

questions.question: Which famous river flows north through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea?
questions.explanation: The Nile has supported life in Egypt for thousands of years.

questions.question: Which is the largest continent by land area?
questions.explanation: Asia is the largest continent in both area and population.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as the capital, partly as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

questions.question: What is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from sea level?
questions.explanation: Mount Everest, on the border of Nepal and China, rises about 8,849 meters above sea level.

questions.question: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation: The Sahara covers much of North Africa and is the largest hot desert.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation: Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, is Canada's capital.

questions.question: Which is the largest country in the world by land area?
questions.explanation: Russia spans 11 time zones across Europe and Asia.

questions.question: Which U.S. state is made up entirely of islands?
questions.explanation: Hawaii is a chain of volcanic islands in the Pacific Ocean.

questions.question: The equator passes through which of these countries?
questions.explanation: The equator crosses northern Brazil, near the mouth of the Amazon River.

questions.question: The Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, lies off the coast of which country?
questions.explanation: The Great Barrier Reef stretches along the coast of Queensland, Australia.

questions.question: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
questions.explanation: Vatican City, surrounded by Rome, covers less than half a square kilometer.

questions.question: Which of these countries has territory on both the European and Asian continents?
questions.explanation: Turkey spans both continents, with the city of Istanbul sitting on each side of the Bosporus Strait.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Japan?
questions.explanation: Tokyo has been Japan's capital since 1868; before that, the imperial capital was Kyoto.

questions.question: How many continents are there, according to the model most commonly taught in U.S. schools?
questions.explanation: The common seven-continent model is Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

questions.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
questions.explanation: There are eight planets; Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
questions.explanation: Gold's symbol, Au, comes from the Latin word "aurum." (Ag is silver!)

questions.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth?
questions.explanation: Diamond, made of tightly bonded carbon atoms, scores a 10 on the Mohs hardness scale.

questions.question: What is the largest planet in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is so big that more than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

questions.question: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explanation: A hexagon has six sides — just like the cells of a honeycomb.

questions.question: At sea level, at what temperature in degrees Celsius does water boil?
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C (212°F) at sea level.

questions.question: Which artist painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s; it hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

questions.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air to perform photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide, water, and sunlight to make sugar, releasing oxygen.

questions.question: How many bones are in the typical adult human body?
questions.explanation: Adults have 206 bones; babies start with more, and some fuse together as they grow.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: The skin is the body's largest organ, protecting everything inside.

questions.question: Who wrote the play "Romeo and Juliet"?
questions.explanation: William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the 1590s.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star! The next closest, Proxima Centauri, is over 4 light-years away.

questions.question: At sea level, what is the freezing point of water in degrees Fahrenheit?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 32°F, which equals 0°C.

questions.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide (rust) in its soil gives Mars its reddish color.

questions.question: How many minutes are in one full day?
questions.explanation: 24 hours × 60 minutes = 1,440 minutes.
